I think they should be paid for going to school. The better they do, the more they're paid.

Many students already are paid for academic excellence - the problem is, for many reasons, it doesn't work out quite as planned.

The Harvard economist Roland Fryer had encouraged four different cities to carry out an experiment on students; Essentially, students were either paid for better academic indicators of performance, or they were not. It was discovered that, despite bribes for performance of up to 200 dollars per student, academic performance remained largely the same.

There was an experiment in Dallas, Texas. Kids were paid to read books. 2 Dollars per book, again if I recall correctly. It worked, in a way; kids did read more books, but they also began to read thinner books. In fact, it was speculated that, if you counted by words instead of by book, the kids might have even been reading less than before. The original incentive to read had become crowded out by the incentive to earn money, and cancelling the monetary incentive at this point, might have even led to them to stop reading completely.

I think that paying kids for better grades isn't as simple as many people assume it is. A monetary incentive cannot simply be added on top of all the other existing incentives for school performance; adding an extra incentive will crowd out other incentives if it's not done properly, and right now, we simply do not have a sufficient understanding of psychological motivations to properly implement extra incentives on anything without affecting the original incentives. A more recent experiment, in paying kids to go to school, has received a bit of success in that attendance rates went up, though academic performance on standardized tests were not significantly affected. It suggests, at least, that it is possible for people to design monteray incentives that motivate kids to do the right thing, though again, the question of crowding out is a huge worry - are the kids going to school for the money, and are kids that originally went to school because school now doing it for the money too? If we now remove the monetary incentive, are kids going to stop going to school, and will attendance rates fall below what they originally were before the incentives?

Who knows? They're pretty difficult questions. Until someone can conclusively answer the above, I don't think it's a wise move to start paying kids en masse to go to school.
